APPROVAL OF MINUTES
  EL MONTE CITY COUNCIL REGULAR MEETING
  OF FEBRUARY 2, 2021

MEETING JOINTLY AND REGULARLY WITH THE EL MONTE HOUSING AUTHORITY; EL
MONTE PUBLIC FINANCING AUTHORITY; EL MONTE WATER AUTHORITY; EL MONTE
PARKING AUTHORITY; SUCCESSOR AGENCY TO THE FORMER EL MONTE COMMUNITY
REDEVELOPMENT AGENCY; HOUSING SUCCESSOR AGENCY; AND, FROM TIME TO
TIME, SUCH OTHER BODIES OF THE CITY WHOSE MEMBERSHIP IS COMPOSED
EXCLUSIVELY OF THE MEMBERSHIP OF THE CITY COUNCIL

1.  CALL TO ORDER: 6:01 p.m.

2.  ROLL CALL FOR CITY COUNCIL AND AUTHORITY BODIES:

  Jessica Ancona, Mayor/Chair – present
  Maria Morales, Mayor Pro Tem/Authority Member – present
  Martin R. Herrera, Councilmember/Authority Member – present
  Victoria Martinez Muela, Councilmember/Authority Member – present

3.  APPROVAL OF AGENDA:

  WITH THE FOLLOWING EDITS/CHANGES TO THE AGENDA:

  SPECIALLY ADDED REGULAR AGENDA ITEM:

  14.16 Consideration and Approval of an Emergency Roofing Project for the Police
  Department Main Building.

  RECOMMENDATION OF BUSINESS ITEM UNDER CONSIDERATION:

  It is recommended that the City Council:

  1. Consider and approve the funding budget for an emergency roofing project at
  the Police Department Main Building for an amount not-to-exceed $350,000;
  2. Authorize the City Manager or her designee to execute an emergency
  Contract Service Agreement for the roofing project;
  3. Authorize an increase in appropriation in the amount of $200,000 in the Asset
  Forfeiture Fund (259) for the FY 2020-2021 fiscal budget to Expenditure
  Account Number 259-71-711-8116; and authorize the use of Asset Forfeiture
  Funds for this supplemental budget appropriation; and
  4. Authorize an increase in appropriation in the amount of $150,000 in the
  General Fund (100) for FY 2020-2021 fiscal budget to Expenditure Account
  Number 100-67-673-8116; and authorize the use of General Fund Reserves
  for this supplemental budget appropriation.

4.  CLOSED SESSION:

  The City Council and the various Authority Bodies whose membership is composed
  exclusively of the membership of the City Council (collectively, the “Council”) will attempt
  to address and complete all Closed Session business between 6:00 p.m. and 7:00 p.m.
  If the Council completes all Closed Session business prior to 7:00 p.m., the Council will
  take a short recess and commence all Open Session proceedings promptly at 7:00 p.m.
  In the event the City Council is unable to address or complete all agendized Closed
  Session items by 7:00 p.m., the Council will hear all such remaining items toward the
  end of the meeting, immediately following Council Communications. Should any member
  of the public wish to address the Council on any agendized Closed Session matter, the
  Council shall allow such person to address the Council on such matter prior to going into
  Closed Session, provided that all persons wishing to address the Council on an
  agendized Closed Session matter shall fill out a speaker card and be subject to a
  speaker’s time limit of 3 minutes per speaker and further provided that the Council shall
  be under no obligation to respond to or deliberate upon any specific questions or
  comments posed by a speaker or take action on any issue raised by a speaker beyond
  such action as the City Council may be lawfully authorized to take on an agendized
  Closed Session matter pursuant to the Brown Act (Govt. Code Section 54950 et seq.).

8.  PUBLIC COMMENT REGARDING NON-AGENDIZED MATTERS:

  This time has been set aside for persons in the audience to make comments or inquiries
  on matters within the general subject matter jurisdiction of the City Council, the Housing
  Authority, the Financing Authority and/or the Water Authority (collectively, the “Council”)
  that are not listed on this agenda. Although no person is required to provide their
  name and address as a condition to attending a Council meeting, persons who wish to

  4
   City Council Meeting Minutes of February 2, 2021

address the Council are asked to state their name and address. Each speaker will be
limited to three (3) continuous minutes. Speakers may not lend any portion of their
speaking time to other persons or borrow additional time from other persons.

Except as otherwise provided under the Brown Act (Gov. Code Section 54950 et seq.),
the Council may not deliberate or take action upon any matter not listed on this posted
agenda but may order that any such matter be placed on the agenda for a subsequent
meeting. The Council may also direct staff to investigate certain matters for
consideration at a future meeting.

All comments or queries presented by a speaker shall be addressed to the Council as a
body and not to any specific member thereof. No questions shall be posed to any
member of the Council except through the presiding official of the meeting, the Mayor
and/or Chair. Members of the Council are under no obligation to respond to questions
posed by speakers but may provide brief clarifying responses to any comment made or
questions posed. The Council may not engage in any sort of prolonged discussion or
deliberation with any speaker or group of speakers on matters that are not listed on this
agenda.

Enforcement of Decorum: The Chief of Police, or such member, or members of the
Police Department as the Chief of Police may designate, shall serve as the Sergeant-at-
Arms of any Council meeting. The Sergeant-at-Arms shall carry out all orders and
instructions given by the presiding official for the purpose of maintaining order and
decorum at the meeting. While members of the public are free to level criticism of City
policies and the action(s) or proposed action(s) of the Council or its members, members
of the public may not engage in behavior that is disruptive to the orderly conduct of the
proceedings, including, but not limited to, conduct that prevents other members of the
public from being heard when it is their opportunity to speak or which prevents members
of the audience from hearing or seeing the proceedings. Members of the public may not
threaten any person with physical harm or act in a manner that may reasonably be
interpreted as an imminent threat of physical harm. All persons attending the meeting
must adhere to the City’s policy barring harassment based upon a person’s race,
religious creed, color, national origin, ancestry, physical handicap, medical condition,
marital status, gender, sexual orientation or age.

Raul Diaz - I am the owner of Xecora restaurant here in El Monte. It was brought to my
attention of comments made against Mayor Jessica Ancona and Councilwoman
Martinez Muela on Tuesday, January 19th by an anonymous person. I was shocked as
those statements are nothing but LIES. On Tuesday, December 15th at about noon, a
woman by the name of Jackie Morales entered our restaurant and began to harass and
question employees, demanding to know when was the last time Jessica Ancona had
been in the restaurant. She insisted she knew that Jessica had been in the restaurant,
and that she demanded to dine inside with Vicky just a week prior and that Jessica now
had COVID and put others at risk in the restaurant. Her questioning and statements
were similar to all of the lies stated in the public comment of the January 19th council
meeting. The staff, confused, denied that ever happening. Jackie Morales continued to
yell and asked to speak to a manager and stated that she would report us to the City
and have us shut down. We later learned that Jackie Morales, is the niece of former
Councilmember Jerry Velasco. She left her phone number for the owner to call her
back. If anyone is abusing power, it appears to be the FORMER elected council
member Velasco and his family by entering my restaurant making demands of my staff
when they are not in any official capacity to do so. Staff informed me that the last time

  5
   City Council Meeting Minutes of February 2, 2021

  they saw Mayor Ancona was Spring/Summer of 2020 picking up take-out and leaving
  immediately after. My staff was shocked and even fearful not knowing who this woman
  was and immediately called me. Staff informed me that the last time they saw Mayor
  Ancona was Spring/Summer of 2020 picking up take-out and leaving immediately after.
  Mayor Ancona has been a loyal patron of ours over the past two years and has never
  made any special requests or demands. I want the record to reflect the truth of what
  happened at my restaurant.

  Melissa Galvez – Hello, as my last email stated... I am growing concerned for the hate
  that First Works Baptist Church puts out into our City. It is alarming that no City officials
  have found this as concerning as your citizens have. You could do better as a City
  Council Member and El Monte resident. You all owe it to your residents to feel safe in
  their own City. Why is this hate group allowed to put others in danger? Do something. I
  am so ashamed my hometown officials do not even bat an eye. You should be
  ashamed if you are not actively working with your citizens to listen to what is going on.
  Thank you.

  Cosmic J. Menes – As a 69-year resident of our fair city I am writing today to
  congratulate our newest councilman Mr. Herrera on his appointment to the serve the
  friendly City of El Monte. Councilman Herrera I wish you nothing but good fortune and
  success…something easily achieved by not aligning yourself with Mayor Ancona and
  Councilwoman Martinez-Muela. Beware of their saccharine smiles; behind those pearly
  whites lies their deceitful agenda. Moving on to important matters of the city, I am
  pleased to see that the council hosted a prayer event regarding that lovely church
  everyone is talking about. It makes sense that someone who campaigned on bringing
  “Bold New Leadership” to our fair city would do nothing of the sort, offering nothing more
  than thoughts and prayers instead of taking any real action. Mayor Palin you continue to
  make El Monte proud! As for the rest of the council agenda, it’s business as usual,
  lawsuits, infighting over who gets to wear the crown of Vice Mayor, and more soon-to-be
  broken promises. But hey, at least Irma Zamorano wasn’t appointed to the city council.

  Chad Horrell – During these unprecedented times, DoorDash is committed to
  partnering with our local government partners. We are also working closely with
  our restaurant partners to assist. As a direct response to the COVID-19 crisis, we
  have provided more than $120 million in commission relief and marketing
  programs to help restaurants replace lost revenue and remain open for delivery.
  Beginning in mid-March we voluntarily launched a series of programs to support
  the restaurant community, and in April we went further by instituting a 50%

  10
   City Council Meeting Minutes of February 2, 2021

reduction in commissions for mom-and-pop restaurants, plus 0% fees for pickup
and 0% fees for restaurants new to DoorDash through the end of May.
Thousands of Los Angeles County restaurants saved hundreds of thousands of
dollars through these programs. Nationally, we are proud to say that restaurants
on the DoorDash platform were 6 times more likely to stay open during the
COVID-19 pandemic compared to US restaurants as a whole. As restaurants
begin to reopen we are committed to finding support and growth opportunities
that reflect our new operating environment. For instance, through our
comprehensive initiative Main Street Strong, restaurants will be able to create
their own online stores to offer takeout or delivery for a flat-fee and no
commission. Recognizing the hardships smaller local restaurants face, those with
fewer than 5 locations will pay no fees through March 2021. Main Street Strong
also includes a free new web presence option, new delivery and pickup
discounts, and prominent featuring of local restaurants in the app and on
DoorDash.com. We are well aware of the crisis at hand, and have willingly
adjusted our business model to accommodate the needs of our partners. That
said, as a company, we oppose price controls imposed by local governments. As
the City considers a possible ordinance limiting contractual agreements with our
restaurant partners, it is important to understand when and why commissions are
charged. Restaurants that offer delivery through DoorDash agree to pay a
percentage of the order subtotal in exchange for that service. The restaurant and
DoorDash agree to this commission in advance through their contract.
Restaurants also have the option to offer their own delivery, or only offer pickup.
Commissions help put money in workers’ pockets (on average $24/active hour in
LA County) and cover a wide range of costs that the local restaurants would
otherwise have to pay directly if they chose to provide their own delivery. These
include background checks for Dashers that ensure food safety for consumers,
insurance for on-the-job injuries, customer support, and other essential
administrative needs. Overall, this business model protects the interests of our
partners and the communities we serve, and taking them away would hurt the
ability of many restaurants to continue operating in the “new normal” we find
ourselves in. We are well aware that the City of El Monte is considering an
ordinance imposing fee limits on third-party delivery platforms. We have seen
many such ordinances adopted all over the country and we would like to share
some suggestions that will help ease the burden on third-party delivery platforms
while providing restaurants fee relief. 1. The ordinance should allow restaurants
to opt in to optional marketing programs, which help restaurants attract new
customers and drive sales. These programs are optional and restaurants will still
have access to delivery and pickup even if they choose not to participate. We
suggest a mending the definition of “Covered Establishment” to read: “Covered
Establishment” means a retail food establishment with fewer than 10 locations in
the State that offers, in a single commercial transaction over the internet, whether
directly or through third-party food delivery services, the sale and same-day
delivery of food to customers from one or more retail locations within the City. 2.
The commission cap should apply to small, local restaurants, identified as having
5 or fewer locations in the state, not chains. This would protect the small “mom
and pop” restaurants that the City is clearly focused on. We would suggest
amending Section 3(c) to read: Any fee, commission, or cost other than as
permitted in subdivisions (a) and (b), above. However, a covered establishment
may agree to pay a third-party food delivery platform a fee that exceeds the limits
in this section to obtain optional products or services, including, but not limited to,
advertising, marketing, or access to customer subscription programs, in addition

  to delivery or pickup service. We thank you greatly for your efforts to protect
  restaurants. We also thank you for considering these small but important
  changes to the proposed ordinance. Please do not hesitate to reach out with any
  questions, concerns or clarifications.

  Ross Hutchings – We are the California Self-Storage Association, a 501 (c) 6
  non-profit trade association representing self-storage facilities throughout
  California. Self-storage facilities in El Monte stand ready to work with the City to
  address any concerns that the City has concerning lockouts and lien sales in
  self-storage facilities. We know too well the negative health and economic effect
  of this pandemic. As with many other small businesses, many local self-storage
  operators are struggling too. The common misperception is that self-storage
  businesses are owned by large corporations. In fact, more than 80% of self-
  storage businesses are owned by small mom-and-pop operators. We have
  reviewed the proposed temporary moratorium on evictions ordinance (the
  “Ordinance”) specific to the self-storage industry, and respectfully request that

  12
   City Council Meeting Minutes of February 2, 2021

you do not authorize the implementation of the Ordinance. Self-storage leases
are month-to-month, providing customers the opportunity to vacate their property
at any time to avoid additional rent obligations. When self-storage customers fail
to pay, self-storage owners do not use the eviction process. Instead, the lien sale
process set forth in the California Self-Service Storage Facility Act, BPC § 21701,
et seq. (the “Act”) applies. However, a self-storage owner will typically use best
efforts to communicate with the patron in an effort to reach a mutually agreeable
alternative to the lien sale process, such as payment plans and vacating the
space for a fraction of the outstanding bill. Suffice it to say that operators this City
are already working closely with their patrons to mitigate the effects of the
pandemic as they too have experienced first-hand financial hardship during these
difficult times. If these workout efforts are fruitless, self-storage owners will then
begin the lien sale process as a last resort. Please note, at any point during this
lien process and prior to the auction, a self-storage patron may pay any owed
amounts and the self-storage unit will no longer be subject to a lien sale.
Additionally, the self-storage patron has the ability to challenge any lien sale
under the Act. In addition to providing a lien notice to a delinquent customer, the
Act requires that a self-storage owner provide a form declaration in opposition to
the lien sale along with the lien notice for the patron to complete in the event they
oppose the lien sale. This results in not only significant delays afforded under the
Act to the benefit of the patron, but also allows the patron the means, literally at
their fingertips, to stop the lien process. Given the nature of the self-storage
business and existing rights afforded to patrons under the Act, the harm to small
business owners outweighs the benefit to the patrons during this pandemic. In
other words, the Ordinance is simply not necessary. Additionally, if implemented,
the Ordinance likely violates self-storage operators’ constitutional rights under
California law. Thus, again, we respectfully request that you do not authorize the
implementation of the Ordinance. Nevertheless, to the extent Council votes to
implement the Ordinance, please consider revising paragraph 3(A)(1.), to state
as follows (change shown in underline and bold): “Prior to the date of this Order,
the patron paid all rent due to the storage unit operator pursuant to an
agreement.”

is time that we address the situation as earlier this evening we did receive a

several of my Council colleagues have received numerous emails from the
community with growing concerns about First Works Baptist Church and the

included hateful rhetoric against the LGBTQ community and messagonistic

a petition that was being circulated by members of this community to remove this

community and have been in contact with both Pastor Mejia of First Works

L.A. Versus Hate, U.S. Department of Justice, Bienestar, and the Asian Pacific
Mediation Center via zoom with members of the Police Department and El Monte
Elected Officials. The first meeting took place on January 12th and the purpose
was to share de-escalation tactics with the Police Department and the
organizations involved as well as facilitating a roundtable dialogue. The
organizations involved agreed to reach out to the organizers of the demonstration
and Pastor Mejia to offer suggestions and boundaries for peaceful demonstration
and the opportunity to express their views and concerns. The Keep El Monte
Friendly Group voluntarily engaged in discussion prior to the January 17th
demonstration at that time Pastor Mejia did not chose to participate in the
discussions. The second meeting was held on January 15, 2021, with the L.A.
County Organizations, the El Monte City Council, City staff, and El Monte Police

provided an update that they planned for a peaceful demonstration and a

orderly there were several groups involved in a loud yet peaceful demonstration

information that a second demonstration was going to occur on January 24,
2021. A third meeting was scheduled and held prior to the demonstration on
January 22, 2021. El Monte Officials met with the same group of mediators and a
member of the Keep El Monte Friendly Group to discuss the planned
demonstration. The Keep El Monte Friendly Group planned a demonstration in
support of their rights, beliefs, and concerns. Pastor Mejia continued to refuse to

causing damage. The church was also vandalized with obscene graffiti. The FBI
